title: Back stitch
subtitle: A solid, gapless outline stitch worked in reverse
excerpt: Back stitch produces a solid continuous line with no gaps between stitches. Each stitch goes back to meet the end of the last, giving a neat joined outline. It is the tightest and most precise of the basic outline stitches.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), outline stitches chapter (Project Gutenberg #20776). Mrs Beeton, Book of Needlework (1870), back stitch entry (Project Gutenberg #16746).

glossaryTerms.definition: The exact hole in the fabric where the needle enters or exits. Sharing a stitch hole with the previous stitch creates a gapless join.

heroPrompt: Back stitch in dark red stranded cotton on white linen, a straight geometric border line showing gapless joins, close-up, natural light.

content.text: Back stitch works by going backwards to share the
of the previous stitch. The needle emerges ahead of the working position, then enters backwards to meet the end of the last stitch. The result is a continuous joined line with no gaps.
Bring the needle up one stitch-length ahead of the start point (point B).
Insert the needle back at the start point (point A) and bring it up one stitch-length ahead of B (point C).
Insert back at B, come up at a new point ahead. Each stitch fills the gap left by the forward movement.
Keep all stitches the same length for a regular, even line.

items.cause: The needle is not entering exactly the previous stitch hole.
items.fix: Use the tip of the needle to locate the exact previous hole before inserting. Sharing the hole closes the gap.

items.cause: Stitch length too long for the curve.
items.fix: Shorten each stitch on curves. Back stitch follows tight curves well when the stitches are small.

content.text: Back stitch is the base for whipped back stitch, threaded back stitch, and Pekinese stitch. It is also the structural stitch in Holbein stitch.
